title: Formal Essay Upgrade
intro: Also becomes moreover. But becomes however. A lot of becomes a great deal of. Essay polish for Cambridge Part 2 — swap the informal for its formal twin.

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'but'
A2.why: “However” often starts a sentence: “However, the town had no doctor.”

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'also'
A2.why: Use it at the start of a sentence to add a point.

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'so'
A2.why: Shows a result: “It rained; therefore, the rodeo was cancelled.”

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'buy'
A2.why: Common in shops and official letters: “purchase a ticket”.

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'start'
A2.why: Very formal: “The ceremony will commence at noon.”

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'get'
A2.why: Formal for getting something with effort: “obtain a visa”.

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'need'
A2.why: “Patients require rest” sounds more formal than “need”.

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'help'
a more formal way to say 'let'
A2.why: Signs say “Dogs not permitted”, not “Dogs not let”.

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'live'
A2.why: Official forms ask where you reside.

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'tell'
A2.why: “Please inform the reception” is formal for “tell”.

A2.right: a more formal way to say 'many'
A2.why: “Numerous visitors come to Valencia” sounds more like an essay.

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'even so'
B1.why: Accepts one point but continues anyway: “It was risky. Nevertheless, they went.”

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'so' or 'as a result'
B1.why: Introduces a result, usually at the start of a sentence.

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'about'
B1.why: Very common in formal emails: “regarding your order”.

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'enough'
B1.why: “Sufficient water” is the essay version of “enough water”.

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'show'
B1.why: “The study demonstrates…” is classic essay language.

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'extra'
B1.why: “Additional costs” sounds more formal than “extra costs”.

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'before'
B1.why: “Prior to the operation, wash your hands”: formal and clinical.

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'after'
B1.why: Very formal; “after” is fine in most writing.

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'roughly' or 'around'
B1.why: With numbers: “approximately 800,000 people live in Valencia”.

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'ask'
B1.why: British spelling with e: “I am writing to enquire…”.

B1.right: a more formal way to say 'now'
a more formal way to say 'what's more'
B1.why: Adds another point to an argument.

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'also' — adding a stronger point
B2.why: “Moreover” adds a point that makes your argument even stronger.

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'a lot of'
B2.why: Use with uncountable nouns: “a great deal of time”.

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'but' — contrasting two ideas
B2.why: Sets two things side by side to show the difference.

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'try'
B2.why: British spelling with -our: “We will endeavour to help.”

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'help make something easier'
B2.why: “The railway facilitated trade in the West”: it made trade easier.

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'use'
B2.why: British -ise spelling; use it sparingly, “use” is often better.

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'get' or 'obtain'
B2.why: Often for skills or property: “acquire a language”.

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'most of'
B2.why: Takes a plural verb with people: “the majority of doctors agree”.

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'find out'
B2.why: “The doctor tried to ascertain the cause”: find out for sure.

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'bad for'
a more formal way to say 'if'
B2.why: Used for possible situations: “in the event that it rains”.

B2.right: a more formal way to say 'later on'
B2.why: Tells what happened afterwards: “He was subsequently arrested.”

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'despite'
C1.why: Legal-sounding: “Notwithstanding the risks, the surgeon went ahead.”

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'about'
C1.why: Note: “with regard to”, never “with regards to”.

C1.right: the most formal way to introduce a debatable claim
C1.why: Presents an idea without fully committing to it.

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'because of' or 'given'
C1.why: “In light of new evidence”: considering what we now know.

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'a lot'
C1.why: Measures degree: “Antibiotics changed medicine to a considerable extent.”

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'mentioned before'
C1.why: Legal and academic; refers back to something already named.

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'until now'
C1.why: Very old-fashioned and legal; rarely needed in essays.

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'to keep this short'
C1.why: Brevity = shortness; a polite way to cut a list short.

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'from now on'
C1.why: Marks a change: “Henceforth, all saloons will close at ten.”

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'and in this way'
C1.why: Links an action to its result: “He washed his hands, thereby reducing infection.”

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'to explain clearly'
C1.why: From Latin “lux”, light: to shed light on something.

C1.right: the most formal way to say 'we really must'
C1.why: Followed by the base verb: “It is imperative that he rest.”
